reference.source: WHO Classification of Female Genital Tumours; Berek & Novak's Gynecology
clinicalPearls: A malignant ovarian germ cell tumour of children and young women, defined by the presence of immature (usually neuroepithelial) tissue, in contrast to the common benign mature cystic teratoma.
Grading is based on the quantity of immature neuroepithelium, and a widely used two-tier scheme divides tumours into low grade and high grade, which guides the need for chemotherapy.
Serum alpha-fetoprotein may be mildly elevated, and a markedly raised level should prompt a search for a yolk sac (endodermal sinus) tumour component within a mixed germ cell tumour.
Typical presentation is a rapidly enlarging, often large, solid or mixed solid-cystic adnexal mass in an adolescent or young woman, sometimes complicated by torsion or rupture.

Fertility-sparing unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy with surgical staging is the standard operation, since the disease is usually unilateral and preserving the uterus and contralateral ovary is a priority in this young population.

Adjuvant platinum-based combination chemotherapy is highly effective for higher-grade or advanced disease, and many low-grade, stage-confined tumours can be managed with surgery and surveillance alone.

Peritoneal and lymph node deposits should be assessed for grade, and mature glial implants on the peritoneum (gliomatosis peritonei) are typically benign and do not by themselves worsen the prognosis.
Growing teratoma syndrome, the enlargement of mature teratomatous masses during or after chemotherapy with normal markers, requires surgical excision rather than more chemotherapy.
reference.pathophysiology: Immature teratomas are germ cell tumours arising from a totipotent germ cell that differentiates along all three embryonic germ layers but, unlike mature teratoma, retains variable amounts of immature, embryonal-type tissue. The immature component is most often primitive neuroectoderm forming neuroepithelial rosettes and tubules, and the amount of this tissue determines tumour grade and malignant potential. As a germ cell neoplasm of the young ovary, it grows rapidly and can seed the peritoneum; implants may be immature (worsening prognosis) or may mature over time into benign glial nodules. Some tumours coexist with other germ cell elements such as yolk sac tumour, accounting for occasional marker elevation. The tendency of residual disease to differentiate into mature tissue under chemotherapy underlies the growing teratoma syndrome and the general principle that grade of both primary and implants dictates management.
additionalDifferentials: small round blue cell tumours involving the ovary
additionalInvestigations: pelvic ultrasound and MRI to characterise the mass
CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis for staging
histological grading of the primary tumour and any peritoneal implants
beta-hCG and AFP monitoring during follow-up
redFlags: rapidly enlarging pelvic mass in an adolescent or young woman
markedly elevated alpha-fetoprotein suggesting a yolk sac component
acute abdomen from torsion or rupture
enlarging masses during chemotherapy with normalising markers suggesting growing teratoma syndrome
peritoneal or nodal deposits containing immature elements
reference.prognosis: With fertility-sparing surgery and, where indicated, platinum-based chemotherapy, cure rates are high, particularly for low-grade and early-stage disease; prognosis worsens with higher grade, advanced stage and the presence of immature peritoneal implants.
pitfalls: Confusing an immature teratoma with a benign mature cystic teratoma on imaging and undertreating it.
Overlooking a coexisting yolk sac tumour when alpha-fetoprotein is markedly raised.
Grading the primary but neglecting to grade peritoneal implants, which independently affects management.
Treating growing teratoma syndrome with further chemotherapy instead of surgical excision.
Performing unnecessarily radical surgery in a young woman when fertility-sparing resection with staging is appropriate.
